extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of classical philosophy / ethics (general readers of Aristotle)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying Aristotle's criteria for what counts as Friendship (its kinds, requisites, and proper/degenerate forms) as described in the chapters on Friendship and the opening of Pleasure. Useful for analysing interpersonal bonds in light of Aristotelian ethics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marks/definitions of Friendship
rubrics_metrics.description: Friendship is characterised by one (or more) of these marks: “one who intends and does what is good (or what he believes to be good) to another for that other’s sake,” “one who wishes his friend to be and to live for that friend’s own sake,” “one who lives with another and chooses the same objects,” or “one who sympathises with his friend in his sorrows and in his joys.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are presented as different diagnostic signs: some friendships are founded on benevolent action, some on wishing the friend's good for the friend's own sake, some on shared life/interests, some on sympathetic response to joys and sorrows. Any of these marks can be used to characterise a relationship as friendship, though full (highest) friendship resembles the self-regarding attitudes of the good man. Examples/notes: mothers (wishing children to live for their own sake; sympathy) illustrate some marks. Use these marks to classify or evaluate particular relationships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Friend as Second Self / Unity with another
rubrics_metrics.description: A true friend is in effect another Self: the good man has toward himself all the marks of friendship, and a friend is 'in fact another Self.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle uses the idea of the friend as a second Self to explain why friends wish for the same things and sympathise. Evaluate friendship strength by the degree to which one treats the friend's existence, concerns, and flourishing as one treats one's own. Intimacy and shared perception of existence (living together in thought/action) are evidence of this unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Goodness as the measure of friendship
rubrics_metrics.description: The good man especially possesses the feelings constitutive of friendship; other people have them only insofar as they regard themselves as good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle ties the quality and depth of friendship to moral character: virtuous persons both love themselves rightly and are thereby capable of genuine friendships. When evaluating a friendship, consider whether its participants are guided by stable, reasoned good rather than transient appetites. Anti-pattern: friendships grounded in vice or instability lack true unity and durable affection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of Sentiment (shared aims in action) — social friendship
rubrics_metrics.description: Unity of Sentiment concerns agreement about matters of action and things important to life (expediency and common interest), not mere unity of opinion about abstract points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this criterion to identify social/political friendship: common decisions about what to do (e.g., choice of magistrates, alliances) and coordinated action indicate unity of sentiment. Distinguish from mere agreement on technical matters (astronomy, etc.), which does not constitute this form of friendship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kindly Feeling as preliminary, not identical with Friendship
rubrics_metrics.description: Kindly Feeling may exist toward persons unknown to us and lacks the yearning and intimacy of Affection; it is often a superficial, sudden liking and can be a dormant stage preceding real Friendship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat kindly feeling as an incipient or superficial marker (pleasure/approval without commitment). It can develop into friendship through duration and intimacy; it is not sufficient alone. Anti-pattern: relationships based only on transient liking or instrumental advantage are not true friendships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Friendship types: pleasure-based, utility-based, and good-based
rubrics_metrics.description: Implicit throughout is the tripartite distinction: friendships can be founded on pleasure, on advantage/use, or on mutual recognition of goodness/virtue (the highest kind).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a relationship, ask whether it is maintained chiefly for pleasure, utility, or the mutual appreciation of virtue. Pleasure and utility friendships are changeable and contingent; good-based friendships are stable, reciprocal, and enduring. Note: Aristotle repeatedly contrasts these to assess who 'needs' friends and why.

rubrics_metrics.name: Benefactor–beneficiary asymmetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who confer benefits often feel more friendship toward the objects of their kindness than the recipients do toward them, because benefactors 'love their work' and value the existence and honour displayed in their benefaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This explains unequal affection in relationships involving giving: creators, benefactors, and parents may feel stronger attachment than recipients. Use this to diagnose one-sided ties and to distinguish affectionate motives from mere gratitude or self-interested reciprocation. Examples: poets and their poems, mothers and children, artisans and their products.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-love: proper (virtuous) vs. vulgar self-love
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a praiseworthy self-love (loving the rational/intellectual Principle and granting oneself what is noble) distinct from the vulgar self-love that seeks wealth, honours, and bodily pleasures; the good man is rightly Self-loving in the former sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate self-directed motives: if a person loves themselves by cultivating virtue and honour (i.e., loving the best part of themselves), this supports genuine friendship (to self and others). If self-love is sensual or covetous, it is blameworthy and undermines true friendship. Use this to distinguish selfishness from justified self-regard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capacity for sympathy with one's own Self as prerequisite
rubrics_metrics.description: The good man can sympathise with himself in joys and sorrows because his desires are unified; the wicked, whose soul is torn by faction, cannot be friends even with themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether an individual's internal unity (consistency of desires, absence of chronic remorse or faction) permits self-friendship; lack thereof indicates incapacity for true friendship with others. Anti-pattern: persons prone to regret, divided desires, or self-directed hatred cannot sustain reciprocated friendship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Friendship's role in the happy (eudaimon) life
rubrics_metrics.description: Even the Happy man needs friends: friends supply objects for benefaction, shared activities for the exercise and contemplation of virtue, and company that makes sustained virtuous activity easier and more pleasurable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging the social needs of a flourishing life, include friendship as an intrinsic good that enables virtuous action and contemplation. Distinguish friends needed for utility or pleasure (less necessary to the Happy) from friends needed for virtue and the enjoyment of living well (essential).

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate number of friends — intimacy limit
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a limited (non-definite) maximum number of friends one can have with intimacy; true intimacy is scarce and cannot be spread equally among many.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use intimacy and the capacity to share joys/sorrows as constraints on friend-count: prioritize a manageable number of close friends rather than many superficial intimacies. Anti-pattern: over-complaisance or attempting intense friendship with many leads to shallow ties.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to call on friends: prosperity vs adversity
rubrics_metrics.description: Friends are especially necessary in adversity (for useful help and comfort); in prosperity they are honourable company and recipients of benefactions. One should call in friends readily in good fortune (if one can forward it) but be cautious about burdening them with one's misfortunes unless their help would be of great use and involves small cost to them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate social conduct: seek friends proactively to share and further good fortune and selectively to relieve misfortune without needlessly implicating them. Also: go unasked and promptly to friends in their misfortunes where kindness is due. Be mindful of appearing sulky in refusing sympathy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intimacy as the essence of true Friendship — shared activity and improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Friendship is essentially communion: friends desire intimacy (sharing words, thoughts, and life) and practise shared activities (drinking, hunting, philosophical study) which produce mutual improvement; the friendship of good men grows by intercourse and mutual correction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge friendships by the degree of shared life and reciprocal moral influence. True friendships involve repeated interaction and mutual shaping toward the good. Anti-pattern: friendships that only involve co-presence or instrumental cooperation without personal sharing do not reach Aristotle's ideal of friendship.
